short: Wave after wave of Gothic raiding overran the Balkans and Aegean for two decades before Rome regained the initiative.
full:
From 250 CE, Gothic coalitions under the king Cniva crossed the Danube in force, defeating and killing the emperor Decius in battle in 251 — the first Roman emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy. Further raiding followed through the 250s and 260s, striking as far as Asia Minor and the Aegean; in 267 a fleet of Heruli and Goths sacked Athens itself, destroying much of the city despite its recently rebuilt walls, and was driven off only by citizens organised under the historian Dexippus.

The invasions reached their peak in 267–268, when a vast coalition moved by land and sea into the Balkans and Greece. Roman forces broke the coalition's main strength by 269, ending two decades of near-continuous Gothic pressure on the empire's northern frontier and easing, for a time, one of the third century's most persistent threats.
